Q000606.stem: Uploads to a bucket must trigger two independent consumers: a Lambda thumbnailer for .jpg files only, and an audit pipeline for all objects, each able to fail without affecting the other. Which design fits?

choices.text: One S3 notification to Lambda that calls the audit pipeline
Send S3 events to EventBridge; one rule per consumer
A scheduled Lambda that lists new objects every minute
Two S3 notifications with overlapping prefix and suffix filters

Q000606.explanation:
Why this is correct:
With EventBridge, S3 events can be filtered by suffix and delivered to multiple independent targets, each with its own retries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Chained Lambda: couples the consumers, so one failure affects both.
• Polling: adds delay and cost.
• Overlapping notification filters: S3 rejects overlapping filters for the same event type.

Key takeaway: fan-out and filtering of S3 events → EventBridge.

Q000650.stem: Internal microservices on ECS need mutual TLS with certificates trusted only inside the company, issued automatically and rotated frequently. Which service fits?

choices.text: KMS asymmetric keys used as certificates
AWS Private CA issuing short-lived private certificates
ACM public certificates with DNS validation
Self-signed certificates generated by each service and stored in S3

Q000650.explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Private CA issues private certificates for internal names and clients, can issue short-lived certificates, and integrates with services and automation. Public CAs can't issue for private-only names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public ACM: for public domains; not client certificates for internal mTLS.
• Self-signed: no trust chain management or automation.
• KMS keys: keys, not X.509 certificates.

Key takeaway: internal trust → a private CA.

Q000724.stem: A stack is stuck in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED because a resource was deleted manually. The team needs the stack usable again without deleting it. Which action fits?

choices.text: Edit the stack state in the console's resource list
ContinueUpdateRollback, skipping the resource
Delete and recreate every resource from scratch
Wait for CloudFormation to retry automatically

Q000724.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ContinueUpdateRollback resumes the rollback, and ResourcesToSkip lets it skip resources that can't roll back (such as manually deleted ones), returning the stack to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Editing state: not possible.
• Recreating: destructive and unnecessary.
• Waiting: it doesn't retry by itself.

Key takeaway: stuck rollback → continue-update-rollback (skip if needed).

Q000590.stem: A Lambda function calls a partner API that returns 429 and 503 errors during bursts. 500 concurrent invocations retry immediately, making things worse, and the function must finish within 10 seconds. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: A fixed 2-second sleep between retries for all concurrent invocations
Immediate retries with the attempt count raised to 10 for every invocation
Capped exponential backoff with jitter, limited attempts within the timeout
Raise the function timeout to 15 minutes so retries always eventually succeed

Q000590.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Backoff spreads retries over time, jitter desynchronizes the 500 callers, and capping delay and attempts keeps total time within the 10-second budget.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Immediate retries: amplify load on a struggling dependency.
• Fixed sleep: callers still retry in synchronized waves.
• 15-minute timeout: breaks the 10-second requirement and ties up concurrency.

Key takeaway: retry budget = backoff + jitter + caps that fit the latency target.

Q000597.stem: A developer needs to upgrade a Java 8 service to Java 17, generate unit tests for it, and ask questions about the AWS SDK, all inside VS Code. Which tool fits?

choices.text: The Amazon Bedrock console playground with pasted code
Amazon Q Developer in the IDE
AWS Cloud9 with no AI assistant enabled
Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer comments on pull requests

Q000597.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Q Developer integrates with IDEs such as VS Code, offering code transformation (including Java upgrades), unit test generation, explanations, and AWS guidance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeGuru Reviewer: reviews PRs; no transformation or test generation in the IDE.
• Cloud9 without AI: just an editor.
• Bedrock playground: no IDE or project integration.

Key takeaway: IDE-native AI for transform, test, and explain → Q Developer.

Q000601.stem: A VPC-attached Lambda function must query RDS in private subnets and also call the public Stripe API. It currently reaches RDS but times out calling Stripe. What fixes this?

choices.text: Assign the Lambda function a public IP address in a public subnet
Add an internet gateway route to the function's private subnets
Remove the function from the VPC so it can reach both services
Route the function's private subnets to a NAT gateway

Q000601.explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC-attached Lambda ENIs have private IPs only. Internet access requires the function's subnets to route through a NAT gateway (in a public subnet), while RDS remains reachable privately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IP: Lambda ENIs don't get public IPs, even in public subnets.
• IGW route from private subnets: doesn't work without public IPs.
• Leaving the VPC: loses private access to RDS.

Key takeaway: VPC Lambda + internet = NAT gateway.

Q000608.stem: An SNS-invoked Lambda function sometimes throws on malformed messages. The team wants failed events kept with error details, and wants to stop after 1 retry instead of the default. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Switch the trigger to synchronous invocation
Wrap the handler in try/catch and swallow all errors
Configure a DLQ on the function with default retries
Max retries 1 plus an on-failure destination

Q000608.explanation:
Why this is correct:
For asynchronous invocations, Lambda retries twice by default. The asynchronous configuration can reduce retries and set an on-failure destination, which records the event plus error details (richer than a DLQ).

Why the other options are wrong:
• DLQ with defaults: keeps 2 retries, and the DLQ stores only the event.
• Swallowing errors: loses failures silently.
• Synchronous: SNS invokes Lambda asynchronously.

Key takeaway: async failures → tune retries + on-failure destination.

Q000611.stem: A developer wants to test a deployed function with a sample SQS batch payload repeatedly, and share the same test event with teammates, without writing code. Which feature fits?

choices.text: AWS Config rules evaluating the function's settings
X-Ray traces from previous invocations
Shareable test events in the Lambda console
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries on the function

Q000611.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Lambda console Test tab runs a function with a saved JSON event, including templates for services such as SQS. Shareable test events let teammates reuse them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights: analyzes logs; doesn't invoke.
• Config: evaluates configuration.
• X-Ray: observes past invocations; doesn't invoke.

Key takeaway: quick manual invokes → console test events.

Q000616.stem: A checkout reads an item right after writing it and sometimes sees the old value. The read uses GetItem on the base table. What change guarantees the latest value, and what does it cost?

choices.text: Read from a GSI, which is always strongly consistent
ConsistentRead=true; uses twice the read capacity
Enable DynamoDB Streams to force consistency
Use a Scan, which returns the newest version

Q000616.explanation:
Why this is correct:
GetItem is eventually consistent by default. Setting ConsistentRead=true returns the latest committed value from the base table and consumes twice the read capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GSI: supports only eventually consistent reads.
• Scan: also eventually consistent by default, and expensive.
• Streams: capture changes; they don't change read consistency.

Key takeaway: strong reads = base table + ConsistentRead, at 2× RCU.

Q000619.stem: An Orders table uses partition key customerId and sort key orderDate. A report needs all orders from last month across all customers, run hourly, and the current Scan is expensive. Which fix fits?

choices.text: Strongly consistent Scan reads
A Query using only a filter on orderDate
A parallel Scan with more segments and a filter on orderDate
A GSI keyed on order month with orderDate sort; Query it

Q000619.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Query needs a partition key value. A GSI keyed by month (for example, 'YYYY-MM') lets the report query one partition with a sort key range instead of reading the whole table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Query without a partition key: not possible.
• Parallel Scan: faster, but still reads and pays for every item.
• Consistent Scan: costs more and still reads everything.

Key takeaway: design keys (or GSIs) for the access pattern; avoid Scans for regular reports.

Q000623.stem: A table stores chat messages. The app must fetch the latest 20 messages in a room, newest first, efficiently. Which key design fits?

choices.text: Partition key messageId only, then Scan and sort in code
Partition key roomId, sort key timestamp; Query descending, limit 20
Partition key roomId only, with the timestamp as a regular attribute
Partition key timestamp, sort key roomId

Q000623.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A composite key groups items by roomId and orders them by timestamp. A Query with ScanIndexForward=false and Limit=20 returns the newest messages efficiently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• messageId + Scan: reads the whole table.
• Timestamp partition: scatters a room's messages and creates hot keys.
• roomId only: one item per room, since keys must be unique.

Key takeaway: partition = the group you query by; sort = the order you need.

Q000625.stem: A developer's DynamoDB code is full of type descriptors like {"S": ...} and {"N": ...} and bugs from converting numbers. Which change reduces this boilerplate?

choices.text: Use the SDK's document client or object mapper
Store every attribute as a string to avoid types
Use BatchWriteItem for all writes
Switch to PartiQL so types are no longer needed

Q000625.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Document clients and object mappers (such as the AWS SDK Enhanced Client or DynamoDB Document Client) convert native types to and from DynamoDB's attribute-value format automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All strings: loses numeric sorting and arithmetic.
• PartiQL: still returns typed attribute values from the low-level API.
• BatchWriteItem: about batching, not types.

Key takeaway: let the higher-level client handle marshalling.

Q000630.stem: A product catalog lives in DynamoDB. Users need fuzzy full-text search with relevance ranking and facets. Which design fits?

choices.text: Move the catalog to S3 and query with Athena per request
Scan with contains() filters on each request
Add GSIs for every searchable word
Stream changes into OpenSearch Service and search there

Q000630.explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpenSearch provides full-text search, fuzzy matching, relevance scoring, and aggregations (facets). DynamoDB Streams, or the zero-ETL integration, keeps the index in sync while DynamoDB stays the system of record.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scan with contains(): slow, expensive, and no relevance ranking.
• GSIs per word: impractical and not full-text.
• Athena per request: too slow for interactive search.

Key takeaway: full-text search → OpenSearch alongside the primary database.

Q000633.stem: A web app needs username and password sign-up, MFA, social login with Google, and JWTs for its API. Which service fits?

choices.text: A Cognito identity pool alone
A Cognito user pool with Google federation and MFA
IAM Identity Center for customers
IAM users created for each customer with console passwords

Q000633.explanation:
Why this is correct:
User pools are user directories that handle sign-up, sign-in, MFA, and social or SAML federation, and issue JWTs (ID and access tokens) the API can validate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity pools: issue AWS credentials; they aren't a user directory.
• IAM users: not for app end users.
• Identity Center: workforce access to AWS, not customer apps.

Key takeaway: app users and JWTs → user pool; AWS credentials → identity pool.

Q000636.stem: An API accepts bearer tokens in the Authorization header. A token leaked in a public log. What does this mean, and which mitigation fits BEST?

choices.text: It is safe because tokens are encrypted with KMS
Anyone holding it can use it; shorten expiry, revoke tokens
Nothing, since bearer tokens are bound to the original client's IP
It is unusable without the user's password

Q000636.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bearer tokens grant access to whoever presents them. Keep access tokens short-lived, revoke refresh tokens (Cognito supports token revocation), and never log tokens.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IP binding: not a property of bearer tokens.
• Password needed: the token itself is the credential.
• KMS encryption: the token is signed, and possession is what matters.

Key takeaway: bearer = possession; minimize lifetime and exposure.

Q000640.stem: A build server in another cloud currently uses an IAM user's access keys to deploy to AWS. Security wants no long-term credentials. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Rotate the IAM user's access keys weekly
Create a second IAM user for backup deployments
Store the keys in Secrets Manager on the build server
OIDC federation to an IAM role

Q000640.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Roles have no long-term credentials. Trusting the build system's OIDC provider lets it exchange its identity token for temporary role credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Weekly rotation: still long-term keys.
• Second user: more long-term keys.
• Secrets Manager: stores keys but doesn't make them temporary.

Key takeaway: users hold long-term keys; roles give temporary credentials.

Q000643.stem: An API must authorize requests using a partner's proprietary HMAC header, and cache decisions for 5 minutes to reduce latency. Which API Gateway feature fits?

choices.text: An API key with a usage plan and throttling per partner
IAM authorization with SigV4
A Cognito user pool authorizer
A Lambda authorizer (request type) with result caching

Q000643.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda authorizers run custom logic, such as validating a proprietary signature, return an IAM policy, and can cache results by identity source for a TTL.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cognito authorizer: validates Cognito JWTs only.
• IAM SigV4: requires AWS credentials.
• API keys: identify clients for quotas; not authentication.

Key takeaway: custom auth schemes → Lambda authorizer.

Q000646.stem: A role's only policy allows dynamodb:GetItem on table Orders. The function also calls Query on Orders and PutItem on Audit. What happens?

choices.text: Everything is allowed since there's no explicit Deny
All DynamoDB actions are allowed on Orders
Only GetItem on Orders succeeds
GetItem is denied because a Deny is required first

Q000646.explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM denies by default. Only explicitly allowed actions on the listed resources succeed; Query and PutItem have no allow statement, so they're implicitly denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All actions on Orders: GetItem doesn't imply Query.
• No explicit Deny means allow: the default is deny.
• Deny required: allows work without any deny statement.

Key takeaway: default deny; grant each needed action explicitly.

Q000653.stem: A company must ensure that AWS never has access to plaintext customer files, even though they are stored in S3. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SSE-C, with the key sent on each request
SSE-S3 default encryption with S3-managed keys on the bucket
Client-side encryption with keys held only by the company
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key

Q000653.explanation:
Why this is correct:
With client-side encryption, data is encrypted before upload with keys AWS never receives, so S3 stores only ciphertext.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-KMS: S3 decrypts using KMS on authorized reads, so AWS systems handle plaintext.
• SSE-S3: AWS manages the keys.
• SSE-C: the key is sent to S3 on each request, so S3 handles plaintext and key in memory.

Key takeaway: 'AWS must never see plaintext' → client-side encryption.

Q000658.stem: An auditor asks how data moving between a Lambda function and DynamoDB is protected, and whether traffic can avoid the internet. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: Protected only when the function runs outside a VPC
TLS by default; a gateway endpoint keeps it private
Encrypted only if the table uses a customer managed key
Plaintext unless the client enables TLS

Q000658.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB API endpoints use HTTPS/TLS. For VPC-attached functions, a DynamoDB gateway endpoint keeps traffic on the AWS network instead of going through a NAT gateway to the public endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Plaintext by default: endpoints are HTTPS.
• CMK: at-rest encryption, not transit.
• Outside a VPC: TLS applies either way.

Key takeaway: transit = TLS; private path = VPC endpoint.

Q000660.stem: All EBS volumes for a workload must be encrypted with a customer managed key, and a snapshot must be restorable in a DR account. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Enable S3 default encryption on the snapshot bucket
Use the AWS managed aws/ebs key and share the snapshot
Encrypt files in the OS and keep volumes unencrypted
CMK encryption; share snapshot and key

Q000660.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS encryption with a customer managed key covers volumes and snapshots. Sharing an encrypted snapshot requires sharing the snapshot and granting the other account use of the key; the AWS managed key can't be shared.

Why the other options are wrong:
• aws/ebs: snapshots encrypted with it can't be shared cross-account.
• OS-level only: volumes and snapshots stay unencrypted.
• S3 encryption: you don't manage the storage behind EBS snapshots.

Key takeaway: cross-account encrypted snapshots need a shareable CMK.

Q000661.stem: A team is classifying data fields for a privacy review. Which field is personal data on its own or in combination, and needs protection?

choices.text: The API version number returned in headers
A customer's name with their home address
A server log's timestamp format string
The AWS Region name where a service is deployed

Q000661.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A name combined with an address identifies a person and is personally identifiable information, requiring controls such as encryption, masking, and access limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• API version, Region name, timestamp format: technical metadata that doesn't identify a person.

Key takeaway: PII = data that identifies a person, alone or combined.

Q000663.stem: A function's environment variables hold a third-party API key. Security requires that only the function's role can decrypt it and that decryption is logged. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Rely on the default AWS managed key encryption
Store the key in plaintext and restrict console access
Base64-encode the value before saving it
A CMK whose policy allows only that role

Q000663.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda encrypts environment variables at rest with an AWS managed key by default. Using a customer managed key lets the key policy restrict who can decrypt, and CloudTrail logs KMS usage. For sensitive values, consider encryption helpers or Secrets Manager.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default key: anyone who can view the function configuration can see the values.
• Console restrictions: plaintext is still exposed via APIs.
• Base64: encoding, not encryption.

Key takeaway: control who can decrypt → a customer managed key.

Q000665.stem: An app has database credentials hardcoded in source. Which TWO benefits would moving them to Secrets Manager provide? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Scheduled rotation without code changes
IAM-controlled, audited access to each secret
Automatic scaling of the database
Conversion of NoSQL schemas to relational
Free, unlimited API calls

Q000665.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager controls access with IAM and resource policies, logs retrieval in CloudTrail, and rotates credentials on a schedule using managed or custom Lambda rotation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scaling: unrelated.
• Free API calls: API calls are billed.
• Schema conversion: unrelated.

Key takeaway: secrets out of code → access control, audit, and rotation.

Q000673.stem: Developers need a copy of production data in staging for realistic testing, but must not see real customer names, emails, or card numbers. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Copy the data as-is and restrict it with IAM
Encrypt staging with the production KMS key
Give developers read access to production instead
Anonymize or tokenize PII in the copy

Q000673.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Masking or tokenizing sensitive fields before the data reaches lower environments removes exposure while keeping data realistic. Tools such as Glue DataBrew or custom ETL can do this.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Production access: exposes real PII.
• Encryption: authorized readers still see plaintext.
• IAM on raw data: developers with access still see PII.

Key takeaway: protect PII by transforming it, not only by restricting it.

Q000674.stem: One Lambda package runs in dev, test, and prod with different database endpoints. Prod values change occasionally without redeploying. Which TWO approaches fit? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Put the values in the execution role's trust policy
Embed the values in the zip package
Read values from Parameter Store at runtime (with caching)
Hardcode the values in the source code
Set per-environment environment variables

Q000674.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Environment variables separate configuration per function or stage. Parameter Store lets values change without a deployment when read at runtime with sensible caching.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hardcoding or embedding: require rebuilds per environment.
• Trust policy: defines who can assume the role, not configuration.

Key takeaway: externalize configuration from the artifact.

Q000675.stem: Running sam build in a subdirectory fails with 'Template file not found'. The template is at infra/app.yaml. What fixes it?

choices.text: Commit the template to CodeCommit first
Use sam build --template-file infra/app.yaml
Rename the template to template.json in any folder
Move the template into .aws-sam/build

Q000675.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The SAM CLI looks for template.yaml (or template.yml) in the current directory by default. Point it to another location with --template-file (or -t), or run from the directory containing the template.

Why the other options are wrong:
• template.json elsewhere: still not found in the current directory.
• .aws-sam/build: build output, not the source template location.
• CodeCommit: unrelated to local builds.

Key takeaway: SAM defaults to ./template.yaml; override with -t.

Q000676.stem: A pipeline must start automatically when code is pushed to main in GitHub, but not for pushes to other branches, and without storing a GitHub personal access token. Which setup fits?

choices.text: A developer running StartPipelineExecution manually
A GitHub v1 source action authenticated with a personal access token
A CodeConnections source action on main with a push trigger
An hourly EventBridge schedule starting the pipeline

Q000676.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeConnections (formerly CodeStar Connections) authorizes CodePipeline to GitHub through an app installation instead of a stored token. The source action watches a branch, and pipeline triggers can filter on branch pushes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GitHub v1 with PAT: stores a token and is a legacy action.
• Hourly schedule: not event-driven.
• Manual start: not automatic.

Key takeaway: GitHub + CodePipeline → CodeConnections.

Q000677.stem: A team wants to turn on a new pricing feature for 10% of users, then 50%, then all, with automatic rollback if the error alarm fires, without redeploying code. Which service fits?

choices.text: AppConfig flags with gradual rollout and rollback
Parameter Store with a manual update each day
A Lambda alias with weighted routing
A CloudFormation change set

Q000677.explanation:
Why this is correct:
AppConfig deploys configuration and feature flags gradually according to a deployment strategy, monitors CloudWatch alarms, and rolls back automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store: no staged rollout or automatic rollback.
• Lambda alias: shifts traffic between code versions, not per-user flags.
• Change set: infrastructure changes.

Key takeaway: runtime flags with safe rollout → AppConfig.

Q000683.stem: A developer wants to debug a Lambda handler locally with breakpoints, using the same runtime environment as Lambda. Which command fits?

choices.text: sam local invoke with debug port options
sam package to S3
sam validate on the template, then console tests
sam deploy --guided

Q000683.explanation:
Why this is correct:
sam local invoke runs the function in a Docker container that mimics the Lambda runtime and supports attaching a debugger with debug port options.

Why the other options are wrong:
• deploy: sends to AWS.
• package: uploads artifacts.
• validate: checks template syntax only.

Key takeaway: local runtime emulation → sam local invoke.

Q000685.stem: An API needs dev, test, and prod environments with different backend Lambda aliases and different throttling, from the same API definition. Which API Gateway feature fits?

choices.text: Stages with stage variables and per-stage throttling
Separate APIs copied and edited for each environment
Usage plans alone, without stages
Different HTTP methods per environment

Q000685.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Stages are named deployments of an API with their own URLs, stage variables (for example, pointing to a Lambda alias), and settings such as throttling and logging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate APIs: duplication and drift.
• Methods: not environments.
• Usage plans without stages: plans attach to stages.

Key takeaway: environments of one API → stages + stage variables.

Q000692.stem: A developer wants to test an API locally: send HTTP requests to routes defined in the SAM template and have them hit local function code with hot reloading. Which command fits?

choices.text: sam logs --tail
sam sync against production
sam local start-api
sam local invoke for each route

Q000692.explanation:
Why this is correct:
sam local start-api runs a local HTTP server emulating API Gateway routes from the template and invokes local function code for each request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• local invoke: runs one function once with an event.
• logs: fetches deployed logs.
• sync to production: not local.

Key takeaway: local API emulation → start-api.

Q000698.stem: A team connects its repo to Amplify Hosting. It wants every feature branch deployed to its own URL, previews for pull requests, and password protection for non-production branches. Which setup fits?

choices.text: One Amplify app that deploys only the main branch
Branch auto-detection, PR previews, access control
A manual zip upload to Amplify for each branch
S3 static hosting with a CloudFront distribution per branch

Q000698.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amplify Hosting can automatically connect branches (by pattern), deploy each to its own URL, create previews for pull requests, and restrict access to branches with passwords.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual zip: no CI/CD.
• Main only: misses the branch requirement.
• S3 per branch: rebuilds what Amplify offers.

Key takeaway: branch-based frontend hosting → Amplify.

Q000702.stem: A developer wants unit tests generated for an existing Lambda handler, including edge cases, directly in the IDE, then reviewed before commit. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Use CloudFormation to generate test stubs
Run CodeGuru Profiler to create test files from runtime profiles
Enable X-Ray, which produces tests from traces
Ask Amazon Q Developer to generate tests, then review them

Q000702.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Q Developer can generate unit tests from code in the IDE. The developer should still review and adjust them, especially assertions and edge cases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray: traces, not tests.
• Profiler: performance profiling.
• CloudFormation: infrastructure.

Key takeaway: AI-generated tests speed up work, but review them before trusting them.

Q000706.stem: A Lambda function's dependencies reach 1.2 GB unzipped and exceed the zip limit. Cold starts must remain reasonable. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Increase ephemeral storage to hold the dependencies
Download dependencies from S3 on every invocation
Package it as a container image in ECR
Split the dependencies into five layers

Q000706.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Container images up to 10 GB are supported, and Lambda caches image layers, so larger dependencies are workable. Layers count toward the 250 MB unzipped limit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Five layers: still within the same 250 MB total limit.
• Download per invocation: slow and costly.
• Ephemeral storage: runtime space, not package size.

Key takeaway: large dependencies → container image.

Q000709.stem: A pipeline currently polls CodeCommit for changes and sometimes starts 10 minutes late. The team wants near-immediate starts. Which change fits?

choices.text: Shorten the polling interval to 1 second
Schedule StartPipelineExecution every 5 minutes
Add a manual approval at the start of the pipeline
Use an EventBridge-based change detection trigger

Q000709.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Event-based change detection starts the pipeline as soon as the push event arrives, instead of waiting for the next poll.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 1-second polling: not configurable, and wasteful.
• Manual approval: adds delay.
• 5-minute schedule: still delayed and wasteful.

Key takeaway: prefer event-driven triggers over polling.

Q000712.stem: A team needs instant rollback for a Lambda function and wants callers never to change the ARN they call. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Publish versions; callers use an alias you repoint
Deploy code to $LATEST and redeploy the old zip on failure
Create a new function name per release
Use layers to hold each release's code

Q000712.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Published versions are immutable snapshots of code and configuration. Callers invoke an alias ARN, and repointing the alias to the previous version gives instant rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• $LATEST redeploy: slow, and the old state may not be reproducible.
• New function names: callers must change ARNs.
• Layers: share code; they don't version releases.

Key takeaway: immutable versions + movable alias.

Q000716.stem: A pipeline uploads a new Lambda zip to S3 with the same key each time, and the CloudFormation update shows no changes. Why, and what fixes it?

choices.text: Unchanged key means no diff; use a new key or object version
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration so CloudFormation detects the upload
Delete and recreate the stack every release
CloudFormation never updates Lambda code

Q000716.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation updates function code only when the Code properties (S3Key or S3ObjectVersion) change. Using a unique key (for example, a commit hash) or the object version triggers the update.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Never updates: it does when properties change.
• Transfer Acceleration: unrelated.
• Recreate the stack: causes downtime and is unnecessary.

Key takeaway: change the artifact reference to trigger deployment.

Q000717.stem: During an incident, a developer needs the 20 most recent log events containing ERROR, newest first. Which Logs Insights query is correct?

choices.text: fields @timestamp, @message | sort @timestamp asc | filter @message like /ERROR/ | limit 20
stats count(*) by bin(5m) | filter @message like /ERROR/
fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20
fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message = "ERROR" | limit 20

Q000717.explanation:
Why this is correct:
filter with like /ERROR/ matches substrings, sort @timestamp desc puts the newest first, and limit 20 returns 20 events.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ascending sort: returns the oldest first.
• = "ERROR": matches only messages that are exactly 'ERROR'.
• stats: aggregates counts; it doesn't return events.

Key takeaway: filter → sort → limit.

Q000720.stem: During an incident, on-call engineers must see error rate, latency, recent deploy markers, and related log queries together, across 3 Regions. Which setup fits?

choices.text: An S3 export of logs reviewed after the incident
A cross-Region CloudWatch dashboard
A separate dashboard per Region opened side by side
CloudTrail event history filtered by service

Q000720.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch dashboards can show widgets from multiple Regions, including metrics, alarm status, and Logs Insights results, giving one correlated view.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate per Region: slows correlation.
• CloudTrail: API activity only.
• After-the-fact export: not usable during response.

Key takeaway: one correlated view for incident response.

Q000727.stem: A request intermittently takes 8 seconds. Metrics show the latency spike, logs show a timeout message, but the team can't tell which of 6 services caused it. Which signal should they use next?

choices.text: CloudTrail data events enabled for each service in the request path
More CloudWatch metrics at 1-second resolution
X-Ray traces showing time spent per service segment
Longer log retention on all log groups

Q000727.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Metrics show that something is wrong and logs show events, but traces show where time went across services for a single request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More metrics: still aggregates, not per request.
• Longer retention: doesn't locate the slow hop.
• CloudTrail: AWS API calls, not the request path.

Key takeaway: metrics = what, logs = detail, traces = where.

Q000728.stem: A team has dashboards for known failure modes but spent hours diagnosing a new, unexpected issue. Which improvement reflects observability rather than monitoring?

choices.text: A bigger dashboard with every existing metric
Shorter alarm evaluation periods
More static threshold alarms for known errors
Rich, correlated telemetry for new questions

Q000728.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Monitoring watches predefined signals. Observability means emitting enough high-cardinality, correlated data to ask new questions about unknown failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More thresholds, bigger dashboards, shorter periods: all improve monitoring of known issues only.

Key takeaway: observability = explore the unknown; monitoring = watch the known.

Q000729.stem: An app must publish CheckoutLatency with dimension Environment=Production at 1-second resolution. Metric calls must not slow down requests. Which approach fits?

choices.text: X-Ray annotations as metrics
Synchronous PutMetricData on every request
EMF logs with StorageResolution 1
A metric filter counting log lines

Q000729.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The embedded metric format writes metrics in structured logs, which CloudWatch extracts asynchronously, including dimensions and high-resolution storage, so requests don't wait on API calls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Synchronous PutMetricData: adds latency and can throttle.
• Metric filters: produce standard-resolution counts.
• X-Ray annotations: for filtering traces, not metrics.

Key takeaway: custom metrics without request latency → EMF.

Q000734.stem: A team runs a .NET app on EC2 with SQL Server and wants automatic detection of common problems, with correlated metrics and logs grouped into problem views, with minimal setup. Which service fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch Application Insights
AWS Config conformance packs
Amazon Inspector application assessments
AWS Trusted Advisor

Q000734.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Application Insights sets up monitoring for supported application stacks (such as .NET and SQL Server), detects anomalies, and groups correlated metrics and logs into problems.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration compliance.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.

Key takeaway: app-aware automatic problem detection → Application Insights.

Q000737.stem: A payment function must never be starved by other functions and must avoid cold starts during business hours. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: More memory, which reserves capacity
Provisioned concurrency only, which also caps others
Reserved plus scheduled provisioned concurrency
Reserved concurrency only, which also pre-warms

Q000737.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reserved concurrency guarantees (and caps) a function's share of account concurrency. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized; Application Auto Scaling can schedule it for business hours.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reserved only: doesn't pre-warm.
• Provisioned only: doesn't reserve account concurrency against other functions.
• Memory: affects CPU, not concurrency.

Key takeaway: reserved = guarantee and cap; provisioned = warm.

Q000741.stem: An API behind CloudFront returns different content by Accept-Language. Users see the wrong language. Which fix fits?

choices.text: Add Accept-Language to the cache key via the cache policy
Set Cache-Control: no-store on all responses
Disable compression on the distribution
Rely on ETag headers to separate the language variants in cache

Q000741.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches one object per cache key. Including Accept-Language in the cache policy creates separate cached variants per language (normalizing values helps hit ratio).

Why the other options are wrong:
• no-store: disables caching entirely.
• Compression: unrelated.
• ETag: validates freshness, not variants.

Key takeaway: responses vary by a header → put that header in the cache key.

Q000744.stem: A subscription filter uses the pattern ?ERROR ?WARN on a log group streaming to Kinesis. What reaches Kinesis?

choices.text: Events containing both ERROR and WARN
All events, with ERROR/WARN duplicated
Only events containing ERROR or WARN
Events without ERROR or WARN are deleted from the group

Q000744.explanation:
Why this is correct:
In filter patterns, ? means OR, so events matching either term are delivered. Other events stay in the log group but aren't forwarded.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All events: filters limit what's sent.
• Both terms: that would require an AND pattern.
• Deletion: filters never delete events.

Key takeaway: ? = OR in filter patterns.

Q000745.stem: A Java service's CPU is high in production, and the team wants to find which methods consume the most CPU and latency continuously, with low overhead. Which tool fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch Container Insights
AWS X-Ray service map
Amazon Inspector
Amazon CodeGuru Profiler

Q000745.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeGuru Profiler samples running applications with low overhead and shows the methods using the most CPU and latency (flame graphs), with recommendations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• X-Ray: request flow between services, not method-level CPU.
• Container Insights: resource metrics.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: method-level hotspots → CodeGuru Profiler.
